name: PT Bank Ganesha Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Ganesha — a capital-rich micro-bank priced for a return it does not earn
frontmatter.summary: Bank Ganesha is a small, controlled Jakarta bank with an exceptionally strong capital position and a mid-single-digit return on equity. It has never paid a dividend. The price already capitalises a sustainable return the bank has not earned, while the capital that could fund a higher return sits far above regulatory need with no stated route back to minorities. Sell.
thesis: The franchise earns a mid-single-digit return on equity on a heavily over-capitalised balance sheet, so the funded return is structurally below the cost of equity and nothing in the record changes that path.
Growth is not the constraint and neither is capital; equity is roughly a third of assets and the loan book a fraction of the balance sheet, so balance-sheet leverage cannot lift the return.
No dividend has ever been paid, so the expected return is book-value compounding at a rate below the cost of equity and the minority holder receives no cash return for waiting.
The price capitalises a return on equity well above the one reported, and that gap is the mispricing — the market pays for a re-rating the accounts do not support.
The legitimate upside is a capital return or deployment that puts the cushion to work or hands it back, and that belongs in the bull case rather than the base case.

Control and liquidity are part of the risk — a Hong Kong investment vehicle is the ultimate controlling shareholder and the free float is a quarter of the shares, so the minority cannot force the value out of the balance sheet.

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 results: whether the flat nine-month profit run-rate holds and whether deposit costs keep easing
Annual report: the first dated disclosure of the capital ratio, deposit levels and provisioning coverage
Next annual general meeting: whether the FY2026 profit is retained again, as the FY2025 profit was
Any capital action or follow-through on the Recovery Plan approved at the 2026 AGM

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp31 against a price of Rp84, a total return of -62.9%.** The call is not that Bank Ganesha is a bad bank. It is that the price asks the franchise to earn a return it has never earned, while the balance sheet and the dividend policy guarantee that the minority holder cannot be paid for waiting. The bank reported a return on equity of 6.4% in FY2025 and is running flat in the current year: pre-tax profit of IDR224.6bn in the nine months to September 2026 against IDR290.6bn for the whole of FY2025 describes a book that is growing while earnings are not [S11][S10].

The variant view is precise. A bank that earns a mid-single-digit return on equity, retains everything and never distributes is worth less than its book, not more. The residual-income run says roughly a fifth of book and the justified-multiple method says about a quarter; they are the same statement in different arithmetic [S0]. The market at 0.5x of book is paying for a franchise return closer to nine per cent. Our base case builds the return from the lines the company reports: a net interest margin derived from the reported net interest income and total assets, a cost-to-income ratio near a third, credit cost rising to the through-cycle rate because gross NPL is 1.4%, and a loan book compounding at 9.0%. Nothing in that build produces a return above the cost of equity of 13.0% [S0][S10].

What moves the value is therefore not loan growth. It is the payout and the use of the capital cushion. The bank carries equity of IDR3,689.3bn against a loan book of IDR5,820.0bn, and our estimate puts its capital ratio near 61.8% of risk-weighted assets — a level no commercial bank needs and one the company does not disclose [S0][S11]. If that capital were returned, the minority would own something close to book. The annual general meeting of 8 October 2026 instead resolved to retain the whole FY2025 profit and pay no dividend, explicitly to strengthen capital [S14]; the minority therefore owns a claim on future book that compounds below the discount rate. The bull case is a capital return or a deployment that converts the cushion into earning assets; it carries a quarter weight, not the base case.

Bank Ganesha is a Jakarta-based commercial bank founded in 1990 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange as BGTG, operating from Wisma Hayam Wuruk with a product set spanning savings, current and time deposits, working-capital, investment, housing and vehicle lending, and the usual transaction rails — BI-FAST, QRIS, ATM and mobile banking, foreign exchange and bancassurance [S0]. Its reported segments are banking, consumer, treasury and other, and it employs 290 people, which is the most revealing number in the profile: this is a branch-and-relationship bank with a cost base small enough to run a cost-to-income ratio near a third [S0][S11].

The business model is a spread business on a small book. At the end of FY2025 the bank had IDR5,820.0bn of loans and IDR11,340.4bn of assets, so roughly half the balance sheet is not lending at all but a liquidity and securities portfolio [S8][S11]. Net interest income was IDR418.7bn and non-interest income IDR91.5bn, the classic shape of a small Indonesian bank: the loan book carries the profit and loss and fees are a rounding item, and in the current year fee income has fallen — the nine months to September were roughly a quarter lower year on year, with a weak third quarter after a strong second [S0]. Management's answer is digital: the NEW BANGGA app launched in 2025 with online onboarding, spending tracking and pocket accounts on top of the existing payment rails, and a branch was opened in Denpasar in the same year [S7][S10].

Strategy is twofold and both halves are visible in the record. The first is a cautious retail and small-business lending build — loans grew 15.9% in FY2025 and stood at IDR6,320.0bn at the end of September 2026 against IDR5,820.0bn at the start of the year, with management describing the approach as measured, selective and quality-oriented [S10][S11]. The second is a status build: the shares moved from the development board to the main board of the exchange effective 28 November 2025, and the company has been collecting annual-report and governance awards, which matters for a name that wants institutional money [S7][S10][S2]. Neither half changes the arithmetic of a mid-single-digit return on a very large equity base, and neither is a capital plan: the only capital decision in the archived record is the 2026 annual general meeting's resolution to retain the entire FY2025 profit [S14].

Footprint and positioning are those of a challenger in the smallest size class. With a loan book of IDR5,820.0bn the bank sits in the bottom tier of Indonesian banks by assets, and it competes for the segments the industry aggregates say are growing slowest [S9]. Group and control matter more than the product set. The ultimate controlling shareholder is Equity Global International Limited, a Hong Kong investment vehicle, reported in July 2023 as holding 10.0% directly and a further 23.7% indirectly through PT Equity Development Investment Tbk (GSMF), a group position the press put at 58.7% of the company [S13]. The data pack's undated insider figure of 89.4% and the IDX-IC free float of 24.9% dated 4 November 2026 are not additive: they come from different providers on different bases, and for sizing the minority we use the float, because it is the dated one [S0][S13]. We have no archived evidence that the controller has bought stock in 2026: a press teaser in October reported an undisclosed buyer accumulating a large block of BGTG shares but names neither buyer, price nor date, so we do not treat it as a controller purchase [S11].

What the bank owns, and what that is worth, is the licence plus the capital. A commercial banking licence in Indonesia is scarce and the capital is real; the problem is that both are worth more to a strategic buyer than to a minority holder who cannot force a sale, and the AGM has chosen to retain rather than distribute [S14][S8]. That distinction is the hinge of the valuation in section four and the reason the rating is not a simple asset-value call.

The Indonesian banking system is growing faster than this bank. System lending grew 13.3% year on year in September 2026 while third-party funds grew 8.2% [S9]. The composition matters for a small bank: corporate lending grew 21.3% and state-owned banks 14.8%, while micro, small and medium lending grew only 2.7% [S9]. BGTG's natural segments are precisely the slow ones, so a bank its size lending into small business and consumer credit is running at the pace of its own market rather than losing share [S11].

The structural drivers are the rate cycle and the deposit mix. The house macro deck carries the policy rate at 5.75% into FY2027E with consumer inflation at 3.28%, a combination that removes the funding-cost tailwind of a tightening cycle without delivering an easing one [S0]. For BGTG the funding side is the exposure: at the end of September 2026 time deposits were IDR5,250.0bn of the IDR6,820.0bn deposit base, with current accounts of IDR882.7bn and savings of IDR683.2bn, so roughly three quarters of funding reprices with the market and the deposit beta is high by construction [S11]. That is why interest expense rose faster than interest income in FY2025 and why the margin, not the loan book, is the swing factor in the profit and loss.

Regulation shapes the field in two directions. Capital requirements push small banks either to consolidate or to raise capital, and the 2026 annual general meeting approved a Recovery Plan alongside the profit retention [S14], which is the standing contingency document OJK requires rather than a finding of stress, but is the route by which a capital action would arrive. On the asset side supervision has tightened: the industry conversation through late 2026 has been about restructuring relief and subsidised programme lending rather than about loosening prudential standards [S9]. For a bank with gross NPL at 1.4% and a special-mention book of IDR128.9bn against IDR5,820.0bn of loans, the standard is affordable; it is also what stops a small bank growing quickly through thin-margin segments [S8].

Competitive positioning is best described as licensed and capital-rich but sub-scale. The moat of a small Indonesian bank is its licence, its deposit franchise and its relationships with local businesses; BGTG has a licence and a deposit base but competes against state banks that grew 14.8% in the same period and against digital challengers with a lower cost to serve [S9][S11]. Five forces, briefly: buyer power is high because depositors are rate-sensitive and the deposit mix proves it; supplier power is low, since funding is commoditised; the threat of new entrants is capped by licensing but arrives through digital distribution; substitution is real at the payments layer, where e-wallets take transaction economics; and rivalry is intense in the small-business segment where every mid-size bank pushes the same working-capital product [S9][S0].

The external influences that matter are the policy-rate path, deposit competition and the regulatory class structure that decides whether BGTG must raise capital or can return it. On our macro desk's stance, rate-sensitive Indonesian domestic names are the least favoured exposure in the current balance-of-payments regime, which is a headwind for a bank whose margin is the swing factor [S0]. None of this says the franchise is broken. It says the industry's growth is not available to this balance sheet at a return above its cost of capital, which is the point section four makes.

Market share is small enough to be invisible in the aggregates: a IDR5,820.0bn loan book against a system total measured in thousands of trillions is a rounding error, and the bank's growth depends on its own capital and appetite rather than on any competitive position it defends [S9][S0]. The honest summary is that BGTG holds no durable advantage that would let it earn above its cost of equity, and its capital position makes that absence visible in the return ratio.

*Data note.* This draft works from the FY2025 figures as carried in the press and from the third-quarter 2026 results release. Two lines could not be archived: the deposits level at the end of FY2025 and the split of operating expenses against loan-loss provisions, because the company's investor-relations download links are script-rendered and the financial statements themselves were not retrievable through the registry [S2][S11]. No figure is asserted for either. The model therefore leaves customer deposits and the cost and credit lines unavailable in the history and builds the forecast from the assumptions recorded in the packet. Two figures used below are derived rather than reported and are labelled as such: the nine-month 2026 non-interest income, which is the sum of the data pack's three quarterly lines, and the nine-month 2025 pre-tax profit, which is FY2025 less the FY2025 fourth quarter [S0]. This is a disclosure gap in our evidence, not an estimate dressed as a fact.

Revenue build. Total operating income was IDR510.2bn in FY2025, of which net interest income IDR418.7bn and non-interest income IDR91.5bn [S0]. Net interest income peaked in FY2024 and fell in FY2025 as interest expense rose; pre-tax profit still reached IDR290.6bn because the cost base and the provision charge came down, not because the spread widened [S0]. Non-interest income is the line that has moved most: the nine months to September 2026 booked a derived sum roughly three-tenths lower than the same period a year earlier, because the FY2025 total contains a fourth quarter that nothing in the record shows recurring [S0]. Our forecast takes the nine-month run-rate plus a fourth quarter at the 2026 quarterly average, which is -39.4% on FY2025, and NIM to 3.9% in FY2026E and 4.0% by FY2030E, essentially flat, because the deposit mix leaves no room for a spread surprise and the macro path holds the policy rate at 5.75% into FY2027E [S0][S11].

Margins and costs. The bank is genuinely efficient. A cost-to-income ratio of 33.8% in FY2026E falling to 32.2% is the level implied by the reported nine-month pre-tax profit against the corrected revenue base: the nine-month operating income derived from the data pack, less the reported PBT of IDR224.6bn, leaves operating cost plus provisions as the residual, and the operating cost is what the ratio expresses [S0][S11]. Management points to operating efficiency as a driver of the record FY2025 result [S10]. Efficiency is not the constraint on the return: a bank whose equity is a large fraction of its assets needs an implausible margin to earn a double-digit return on equity. Our modelled return on equity is 6.1% in FY2026E and 6.1% by FY2030E, against 6.4% actual in FY2025 — a flat trajectory built on flat margins and gradual cost improvement, not a recovery [S0].

Credit quality and provisions. Gross NPL was 1.4% at the end of FY2025 against 1.2% a year earlier, and the annual-report detail behind that ratio is IDR81.4bn of substandard, doubtful and loss loans plus IDR128.9bn under special mention [S6][S7][S8]. Our FY2026E credit cost of 0.5% is close to the current NPL flow and rises to 0.7% through the cycle. Two anchors set the long run: the special-mention stock of IDR128.9bn against IDR5,820.0bn of loans, which has not yet been charged, and the charge the FY2025 accounts imply — the reported operating income less an operating cost line at the re-derived ratio and the reported PBT of IDR290.6bn leaves a charge well above the current flow for that year [S0][S7]. The steady state is also the peer book's through-cycle rate for the same industry. We could not source a coverage ratio, so the provision line is an assumption rather than a restatement, and that is the largest analytical gap in this draft.

Cash flow, capital and funding. A bank's cash flow statement is not the analytical object; capital is. Equity was IDR3,689.3bn at the end of FY2025 and IDR3,923.1bn at our FY2026E, with book value per share of Rp154 rising to Rp208 by FY2030E on a zero payout [S0]. Growth is funded internally and comfortably: loans of IDR5,820.0bn against equity of IDR3,689.3bn mean the loan book could double without new capital at any normal risk weight, which is why the estimated capital ratio of 61.8% matters more than any other line and is the least well disclosed [S11]. The company does not publish CAR in any source we could archive, and we flag the estimate as ours rather than the bank's.

Capital allocation and earnings quality. The payout is 0.0% in the forecast and has been zero in every year of the data pack, with dividends per share of Rp0 [S0]. That is not an inference from a vendor field: the annual general meeting of 8 October 2026 resolved to retain the whole FY2025 net profit of IDR227.1bn, allocate a nominal amount to the mandatory reserve and pay no dividend, to strengthen capital [S14], and no dividend policy appears in any archived source. On the earnings-quality screens, the accruals test is not meaningful for a bank, so the relevant tests are provisioning and asset classification: the loan book is classified in detail and the special-mention bucket is disclosed, a positive disclosure signal [S8]. The negatives are structural rather than accounting. Earnings grew while net interest income fell, so the profit record rests on cost control and a lower provision charge rather than on franchise growth, and the shares were upgraded to the main board while the return on equity went nowhere [S7][S0]. The Recovery Plan approved at the same meeting is a standing regulatory contingency document, not a stress finding, but it is the governance item to watch [S14]. Related-party flows could not be quantified from the archived sources and are left as a monitoring item rather than a finding.

The method set is the house bank framework: a justified price-to-book as the primary method and residual income as the cross-check, both discounted at an equity cost of capital built from the sovereign curve and an equity risk premium. This is the right tool for a bank because book value is the capital that generates the earnings, the return on that capital is the observable variable, and the valuation collapses to a single question — does the bank earn more than its cost of equity, and does the minority get paid [S0]. For BGTG the answer to both is no, and the two methods agree on direction even where they differ in magnitude.

The cost of equity is 13.0% with a weighted average cost of capital of 13.0%, since a bank is valued on the equity side with no debt weight [S0]. The build is transparent: the ten-year Indonesian government bond yield of 7.4% less the default spread of 1.6%, plus an unlevered beta of 0.90 times an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, plus an explicit premium of 1.1%. That premium is an equity-risk-premium calibration, not a size or illiquidity add-on: it is exactly the gap between the engine's unpinned CAPM arithmetic and the method card's pinned build for an IDR bank — the sovereign yield plus an equity risk premium at the mid-point of the house band [S0]. No dollar rate is imported into a rupiah valuation. Because the pin is applied at the issuer and not to the peer set, BGTG discounts above the BANKS peer, which runs on the engine default; that gap is the ERP pin disclosed here, not a second charge for the float, and the only marketability adjustment is the house liquidity discount applied to the target.

The primary method is the warranted multiple. At a sustainable return on equity near six per cent, a terminal growth rate set at the house long-run assumption and a cost of equity of 13.0%, the justified multiple of book is 0.2 times, and applied to book value per share it produces Rp36 per share [S0]. The residual-income run, which charges the cost of equity against every year of book value and capitalises the shortfall, produces Rp20 per share — about -44.2% below the multiple method, because a permanent negative spread compounds faster than a single multiple can express [S0]. We weight the multiple at 60% and residual income at 40%, and the dividend discount model at nothing: a zero payout makes a DDM return zero, which is not a cross-check but an arithmetic artefact, and pretending otherwise would drag the target without adding information [S0].

The terminal is where the payout question has to be answered, so we state it explicitly rather than leave it in a formula. Every explicit year to FY2035E carries a zero payout and zero dividends, which is the company's own resolved policy [S14]. The terminal value does not: a warranted multiple with terminal growth of 4.0% against a sustainable return on equity near six per cent is only internally consistent if the bank distributes one minus growth over return on equity — about a third of earnings — from the terminal year. That is a mathematical requirement of the Gordon frame, not a forecast that the dividend starts. The two statements are reconciled by the sensitivity table: at 13.0% the target falls as terminal growth rises, from the zero-growth column towards the top of the growth range, and the zero-payout-forever case is the residual-income method, which is why the DDM carries no weight. If the bank never pays, terminal growth is zero and the value is the low end of that grid; if it pays a third, it is the base case. Neither end of the grid reaches the price.

The divergence between the two methods is the honest content of this section. The multiple method assumes the franchise is worth a fraction of book and stops there; the residual-income method also charges the retained earnings for being retained at a return below the discount rate, which is why it lands lower. We have not forced them to agree. Both say the shares are worth a small fraction of book, and the target of Rp31 against a price of Rp84 is the weighted result, a total return of -62.9% [S0].

Capital and the bridge deserve a paragraph because this is a bank and the arithmetic is different. The engine prints net cash but applies no bridge, and the bridge is deliberately empty: a bank's cash is an operating asset. The IDR6,820.0bn deposit base at September 2026 is funded through that cash and the securities book, which is why assets are still close to twice the loan book [S11]; paying the cash out would shrink the balance sheet and the loan book with it, and the equity that could be returned is already inside the book value that is the numerator of both methods. So the net cash the packet prints is not a distributable surplus and is not added to the value — it is the liquidity buffer. What is genuinely surplus is equity above a regulatory minimum we cannot size, because the bank discloses no capital ratio [S0]. The bull case therefore carries the capital-return path explicitly and with a probability: a reduction in the share count each year funded out of that equity, which is the only mechanism by which the cushion reaches a minority holder at a price above the market's half of book [S0].

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to state the mispricing. At Rp84 the shares trade at 0.5x of FY2026E book, and holding our cost of equity and terminal growth, that multiple is consistent with a sustainable return on equity close to nine per cent, not the 6.4% the bank reports and the 6.1% our model forecasts [S0][S11]. The market is not pricing the bank that exists; it is pricing a bank with roughly half again the earning power per unit of capital. The company would have to lift return on equity by half, permanently and without raising equity, to justify the price — and the one thing the balance sheet shows is that its response to surplus capital has been to hold it [S11][S14].

The reverse view deserves an airing. If the capital cushion is deployed — a buyback or special distribution at half of book, or lending that puts the capital to work at a normal spread — value converges toward book and the negative residual-income tail disappears. That is what the bull scenario prices at a quarter weight: a return on equity path toward eight per cent plus a shrinking share count, which together bring the value within a fifth of the current price [S0]. We keep it out of the base case because no announcement, filing or management statement in the archived record commits to it: the 2026 annual general meeting chose retention over distribution [S14], and the only capital document on file is the Recovery Plan [S14].

The main downside risk is not a credit event; it is the persistence of the current arithmetic. With a return on equity of 6.4% and a cost of equity of 13.0%, every year the bank retains earnings it transfers value from shareholders to borrowers and staff, and the transfer compounds [S0][S11]. Likelihood high, impact high — this is the base case, not the tail.

The second risk is credit, and it is a genuine unknown rather than a modelled certainty. Gross NPL of 1.4% looks comfortable, but IDR128.9bn of special-mention loans against IDR5,820.0bn of loans is a stock that has not yet been classified, and we could not source a coverage ratio to test whether the provision buffer is adequate [S8][S7]. If that book migrates to non-performing, credit cost roughly doubles in our model and the return on equity falls below five per cent. Likelihood medium, impact material.

The third risk is funding. Time deposits are IDR5,250.0bn of the IDR6,820.0bn base, so a competitive deposit market compresses the margin quickly, and our macro desk takes a negative view of Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic names in the current regime [S11][S0]. A margin squeeze of a few basis points a year is already in the base case; a sharper one is the bear scenario. Likelihood medium, impact material.

The fourth risk is structural and specific to this register. A free float of 24.9% on a dated registry figure, against a controlling shareholder that owned the majority of the shares in 2023, directly and through its listed investment vehicle [S13][S0], means the minority cannot force a distribution. The exchange's high-shareholding-concentration screening — which captures issuers whose top ten holders own at least ninety-two and a half per cent [S12] — would matter for how the shares trade, but the archived announcement is paginated and we cannot confirm from it whether BGTG is among the listed names, so we make no claim either way. A rights issue at a discount to book would dilute book value per share and is the standard mechanism by which controlling shareholders of small Indonesian banks rebuild capital; nothing in the record says BGTG will do it, and a bank already capitalised at our estimated ratio has no need of one, so it sits in the bear case rather than the base. Likelihood low, impact high.

Governance and liquidity risks sit alongside. The register is concentrated, the float is thin relative to the IDR2,013.6bn market capitalisation, and a press allegation of problem loans and lost customer funds circulated in the autumn; the article itself concluded that no verified evidence supported an OJK sanction or a customer-funds case, and the loan figures it cited reconcile with the audited NPL [S8]. We treat it as unsubstantiated but note it, because a headline of that kind in a thin float moves the price. Average daily turnover of IDR0.9bn is enough to enter but not enough to exit a position in size without moving the market [S0].

The three scenarios are mirrored in their drivers, as the house requires. Bear: credit cost half a point higher, margin forty basis points lower, loan growth three points lower and the share count rising each year as a discounted rights issue funds a margin the bank cannot earn, with return on equity stuck near five per cent. Base: the most probable path, the one built in section three, with no capital action. Bull: the exact mirror on the operating drivers, plus the share count falling each year as the surplus equity is used to buy stock at half of book, which lifts return on equity toward eight per cent [S0]. The base carries half the probability mass and the two tails a quarter each. The values are not mirrored even though the shocks are: the bear loses more than the bull gains because the warranted multiple is convex when return on equity approaches terminal growth, so the same ten basis points of return on equity is worth more on the downside than on the upside. That asymmetry is a property of the valuation frame, not of the probability weights.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a declared dividend or capital-return plan that puts cash in minority hands; a filed transaction — merger, acquisition or rights issue — that converts the capital cushion into earning assets; a disclosed capital ratio materially below our estimate, which would mean the cushion is smaller than we think; and a return on equity above eight per cent for two consecutive halves without a capital raise [S0][S11]. Any of the first two would move the rating toward neutral or better regardless of the price.

Ownership is concentrated and the register explains much of the valuation. The free float is 24.9% on the IDX-IC mirror dated 4 November 2026 [S0]; the ultimate controlling shareholder is Equity Global International Limited, a Hong Kong investment vehicle reported in 2023 as holding 10.0% directly and a further 23.7% through PT Equity Development Investment Tbk (GSMF), a group position the press put at 58.7% of the company [S13]. We use that dated disclosure for control and the dated float for the minority, because the data pack's undated insider figure of 89.4% overlaps the float and cannot be added to it [S0]. The shares moved from the development board to the main board in late 2025 [S7]. A controlling holder of that size, with a float this thin, sets the price at the margin, and the minority's exit is at that price rather than at the controller's economics. We also note the Recovery Plan approved at the 2026 AGM [S14]; it is a standing contingency document, and the audit trail shows no OJK sanction against the bank [S8].

Board and management have been stable enough to execute a multi-year plan. The president director is quoted across the FY2025 and third-quarter 2026 releases, and the annual general meeting in 2026 renewed the board, appointing a new director and an independent commissioner [S10][S14]. The company publishes an annual report and a sustainability report, quarterly financial statements and risk exposure disclosures through its investor-relations page, and has collected annual-report and corporate-governance awards this year [S2][S12]. For a bank of this size the disclosure is better than the segment average; the gap that matters for us is the absence of a machine-readable capital ratio and deposit level, which is a reporting-format problem rather than an opacity one.

The dividend record is the governance fact that drives the valuation. The 2026 annual general meeting resolved to retain the entire FY2025 profit of IDR227.1bn, allocate a nominal amount to the mandatory reserve and pay no dividend, to strengthen capital [S14]; dividends per share are Rp0 and the forecast payout 0.0% [S0]. No stated dividend policy appears in the archived sources. Related-party exposure could not be quantified from what we could archive, and we flag that as an open item for the annual report rather than assert a number [S2].

Audit and control. The FY2025 figures we use are the audited annual numbers as reported, and the profit figures in the press agree with the data pack to the last decimal, which is a good sign for the quality of the release [S8][S0]. The press allegation of problem loans and missing customer funds circulated in October; the article's own conclusion was that no verified evidence supported an OJK sanction, a customer-funds case or an annual loss, and the figures it cited reconcile with the audited NPL, so we do not treat it as a finding [S8]. We do treat it as a monitoring item, because unverified allegations in a thin float are a price risk even when they are not an accounting risk.

ESG exposures for this bank are mostly governance and social. The environmental footprint of a branch bank is small; the social exposure is lending conduct and the complaint channel, both disclosed; and the governance exposure is control, related-party flows and capital allocation, which is where this name's risk actually lives [S2][S8]. On the house screens the verified structure flags are concentration of ownership and a thin float, with no evidence of a manipulation-class flag.

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar and the corporate-action calendar. Full-year 2026 results, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, will show whether the flat nine-month run-rate held and whether the deposit-cost easing of the last two quarters persisted [S11]. The FY2026 annual report is the first dated opportunity to get the capital ratio, the deposit level and the provisioning coverage that this draft had to estimate [S2]. The next annual general meeting is the event that would change the thesis, because the payout decision is taken there and was taken against the minority this year: the whole FY2025 profit was retained [S14]. A buyback, a special distribution or a filed rights issue would each force a re-underwrite, and none is in the archived record.

The regulatory calendar matters less than it did a month ago. The exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list takes effect in mid-November 2026 and removes the named issuers from index weighting [S12]; the archived announcement is paginated, so we neither claim nor deny BGTG's membership and treat it as a flow issue rather than a fundamental one. Watch instead the Recovery Plan's first progress disclosure, which is where a capital action would surface [S14].

The KPIs we watch, in order: return on equity against the cost of equity; the net interest margin against the deposit mix; the special-mention loan stock and any coverage disclosure; the capital ratio and any capital action; and the payout decision [S0][S11]. A dividend, a disclosed capital ratio below our estimate, or a filed transaction would each force a re-underwrite of this note. Absent those, the arithmetic in section four is the investment case, and it points one way.

bear.narrative: Credit costs normalise toward the special-mention stock as the 2025-26 loan vintage seasons, NIM gives back the time-deposit squeeze and loan growth stalls with the industry. The bank raises equity to defend a margin it cannot earn: three per cent new shares a year, funded at a discount to a book value the market already prices at half, keeps book value per share flat while ROE stays near 5% and the multiple has nothing to hold it.

bull.narrative: The capital cushion reaches the minority: buybacks funded out of equity three per cent of the share count a year at half of book, on top of credit cost half a point lower and NIM forty basis points higher as the loan book takes a larger share of the balance sheet, lifts ROE toward 8% and returns capital while fee income from NEW BANGGA scales. No merger and no named buyer is assumed - none is in the archived record.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 9.0% carries the 8.6% already booked to September 2026 [S11] into the fourth quarter at the same run-rate; FY2027E 9.0% then steps down toward the 8.0% long run as the capital needed to grow faster than ROE x retention is not raised. Sector credit grew 13.26% yoy in September 2026 [S9], so this is a below-market growth plan, not a haircut: BGTG grows with its 290 staff and one new Denpasar branch [S7], not with a corporate franchise.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 third-party funds grew 12.77% [S10]; the plan assumes 8.0% from FY2026E - slower than loans so the loan-to-deposit ratio keeps grinding up from the 92.7% implied by Rp6.32tn of loans against Rp6.82tn of DPK at September 2026 [S11]. Deposit beta is the constraint: the mix is 77% time deposits [S11], so funding reprices with the BI rate rather than lagging it.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: FY2025 1.95x (Rp11.34tn of assets against Rp5.82tn of loans) [F2][F4] falls to 1.72x by September 2026 as the loan book grew and the securities book did not [F3][F5]. The plan glides from 1.78x to 1.70x: the balance sheet stays nearly twice the loan book because the bank holds a liquidity portfolio far above the regulatory minimum.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NIM was 3.86% on average earning assets (NII Rp418.7bn on an average Rp10.85tn) and the nine months to September 2026 were flat: NII Rp326.4bn against Rp325.8bn a year earlier [S0][S11]. Cost of funds is the swing factor - time deposits are 77% of DPK [S11] and the house BI path is 5.75% flat to FY2027E with CPI at 3.28%, so the deposit beta that re-priced upward in FY2025 (interest expense rose 19%) is not repeated. 3.85% rising to 3.95% reflects a small mix shift to loans, not a spread bet.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Non-interest income was Rp91.45bn in FY2025 of which Rp32.97bn landed in the fourth quarter [S0]. The nine months to September 2026 booked Rp41.55bn (Q1 Rp14.11bn, Q2 Rp17.12bn, Q3 Rp10.33bn) [S0]. FY2026E is the nine-month total plus a fourth quarter at the 2026 quarterly average, which is Rp55.4bn, or -39.4% on FY2025: we do not repeat the FY2025 year-end spike because nothing in the archived record shows it recurring, and Q4 would otherwise have to exceed that spike by more than a third. From FY2027E, 6% is fee income from the NEW BANGGA app on the lower base rather than a recovery to the one-off level.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 33.8% is the ratio that reconciles the reported nine-month PBT of Rp224.61bn [S11] with the corrected revenue base (modelled NII plus Rp55.4bn of NOII) and the modelled provision charge: the nine-month PBT against nine-month operating income of Rp368.0bn [S0] leaves operating cost plus provisions of Rp143.4bn, and opex is the residual. The earlier 38.0% was an artefact of inflating NOII to Rp86.9bn. The plan improves to 32.2% by FY2030E as digital onboarding scales; the bank has 290 employees [S0] and management calls efficiency a 2025 achievement [S10], so a flat-to-slightly-better ratio is the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: 50bp in FY2026E rising to 70bp through the cycle. Gross NPL is 1.40% [S6] with Rp81.4bn impaired and Rp128.9bn under special mention at end-2025 [S8] - the special-mention stock alone is 2.2% of loans, so the through-cycle charge sits above the current flow, not at it. The 70bp long run matches the peer book's through-cycle rate for the same industry (AGRS) and is consistent with the charge implied by FY2025: operating income Rp510.2bn less an opex line at the re-derived ratio and the reported PBT of Rp290.61bn implies roughly 80bp that year [S0][S7]. The bank is not releasing provisions; we could not source a coverage ratio, so the steady state is a full-cycle charge rather than the current NPL rate.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default - no recurring non-operating line identified in the archived sources

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: no minority interest on the balance sheet

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero in every modelled year and in the long run. The RUPST of 8 October 2026 resolved to retain the whole FY2025 net profit of Rp227.09bn, allocate Rp1bn to the mandatory reserve and pay no dividend, to strengthen capital [S14]; no dividend has been declared in any year of the data pack [S0] and no dividend policy appears in the archived record. The 0% is therefore the company's own decision, not a forecast device. It is also why the DDM is not a usable cross-check for this name.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default - no rights issue announced; share count unchanged since the 2023 issue

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 1.00x. The bank does not publish CAR in any source we could archive, so equity is measured against a risk-weighted asset base approximated at the loan book itself (loans plus a securities portfolio of similar size, both risk-weighted): equity of Rp3.69tn against Rp5.82tn of loans implies a capital ratio near 63%, the arithmetic consequence of a balance sheet where equity is a third of assets [S0]. This is an estimate and is flagged as such in §4; it is not a company disclosure.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for an IDR reporter (4.0%). The wage: in a Gordon world a 4% terminal growth rate is only sustainable if the bank distributes 1 - g/ROE, which at a sustainable ROE near 6% is about a third of earnings. The explicit years to FY2035E pay nothing [S14], so the terminal value assumes the bank starts distributing then. If it never does, terminal growth is zero and the residual-income value falls well below the base case; both cases are shown in §4.

challenges.challenge: The class-upgrade story does not exist in the archive. The only 'naik kelas' in S7 and S10 is the board transfer Papan Pengembangan to Papan Utama effective 28 November 2025; no source mentions KBMI, core capital, or an OJK adviser urging the bank to move up a class. Yet that story carries the 0% payout rationale ('retained to build a KBMI II-sized base'), the rights-issue risk in section 5 and the whole bull case.
challenges.answer: Struck the capital-class/KBMI story everywhere (sections 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, catalysts, payout basis, rwa_density basis). The only status event in the archive is the board transfer from Papan Pengembangan to Papan Utama effective 28 November 2025 [S7][S10]. The payout rationale is now the AGM itself: the RUPST of 8 October 2026 resolved to retain the whole FY2025 profit to strengthen capital and pay no dividend [S14], a sourced decision rather than an inferred class ambition.

challenges.challenge: 'Prima Tunas has been buying' in the bull narrative appears in no archived source, and section 1's 'block of shares changing hands at a premium to the market' rests only on an S11 related-link teaser (Rp172.31bn of BGTG stock) that names no buyer, no price and no date. A named controlling shareholder and a premium price are asserted as registry facts.
challenges.answer: Struck 'Prima Tunas has been buying' and the premium block-trade claim from section 1, section 6 and the bull narrative. Section 1 now carries the dated control fact instead: Equity Global International Limited holds 10.01% directly and 23.74% through PT Equity Development Investment (GSMF), a reported group position of 58.71% in July 2023 [S13]; the October teaser is described as naming no buyer, price or date [S11].

challenges.challenge: Surplus capital is measured and then thrown away: the model holds net cash of Rp1,026.8bn (Rp42.8/share, 1.3x the entire base-case value) with bridge_items empty, so neither base nor bull credits it. Section 4 concedes that returning it 'would' take the minority close to book. The largest identified upside in the document is assigned a zero weight with no arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Added a section 4 paragraph on capital and the bridge: a bank's cash is an operating asset funding the Rp6.82tn deposit base, so no net-cash bridge is applied and the equity is already inside book value [S11][S0]. The distribution path now has a probability in the bull case: a share-count reduction each year funded out of surplus equity, shocked at 25% weight, which is how the cushion would reach the minority above half of book.

challenges.challenge: Dilution is described as live but never modelled: share_change is 0.0 in every forecast year and the bear shocks only credit cost, NIM and growth. A rights issue at a discount to a 0.53x-book price, the modal capital mechanism for an 89%-held IDX bank, cuts BVPS and is absent from the scenario set that drives the target.
challenges.answer: Dilution is now modelled rather than described: the bear case adds a share_change shock of +3% a year (a discounted rights issue) and the bull mirrors it at -3% a year (a buyback), so share_change is no longer zero in the scenario set that drives the target. The base case stays at zero because a bank at our estimated capital ratio does not need a rights issue, and no capital plan is disclosed [S0][S14].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E NOII is Rp86.9bn under a -5% growth assumption whose stated basis is 'annualise that run-rate'. The nine months booked Rp41.5bn (Q1 14.1, Q2 17.1, Q3 10.3), so Q4 would need Rp45.4bn, 38% above the FY2025 Q4 spike of Rp33.0bn; the run-rate actually implies about -40%, not -5%. The 38.0% cost-to-income ratio is derived from this inflated income line, so the modelled revenue mix is wrong even where PBT reconciles.
challenges.answer: NOII reset from -5% to -39.4%: the nine-month 2026 total of Rp41.55bn from the data pack's quarters plus a fourth quarter at the 2026 quarterly average, instead of a Q4 of Rp45.4bn that would exceed the FY2025 spike by a third [S0]. The cost-to-income ratio was re-derived from the corrected revenue base and falls to 33.8% in FY2026E (opex is the residual against the reported nine-month PBT), with the path to 32.2% by FY2030E.

challenges.challenge: Through-cycle credit cost is set at 60bp, below the same-industry peer AGRS at 70bp, for a sub-scale SME and consumer lender carrying Rp128.9bn of special mention (2.2% of loans) and Rp81.4bn already impaired. The method card requires a full-cycle charge, not a current-NPL rate, and no source is given for 60bp.
challenges.answer: Through-cycle credit cost raised from 60bp to 70bp, matching the peer book's rate for the same industry, and anchored on the charge the FY2025 accounts imply (operating income less an opex line at the re-derived ratio and the reported PBT of Rp290.61bn leaves a charge well above the current flow) plus the Rp128.9bn special-mention stock [S0][S7][S8]. FY2026E stays at 50bp so calibration is unchanged; the target moved with the long run.

challenges.challenge: Both weighted methods assume a 33% terminal payout (warranted P/B (6%-4%)/(13%-4%) = 0.23x) while every explicit year to FY2035E carries payout 0.0 and DPS 0, which is the report's central claim. The multiple is 0.46x at g 0%, 0.23x at 4% and 0.00x at 6%, so the target is a function of one unsourced input rather than of the ROE finding. The DDM, the only method that would reflect the 0% payout, is given zero weight.
challenges.answer: The terminal payout is now stated explicitly in section 4 rather than implied: zero in every explicit year to FY2035E on the AGM's resolved policy [S14], and at the terminal a Gordon-consistent payout of one minus growth over ROE, about a third, which is what a 4% growth rate requires against a 6% sustainable ROE. The sensitivity table shows the target across terminal growth of 3% to 5%, and the never-pays case is the residual-income method at the low end of that grid; the DDM stays at zero weight because a zero payout returns zero.

challenges.challenge: Illiquidity is charged twice. The assumptions add a 1.1pp COE premium (coe_premium) while section 4 asserts 'no size or illiquidity add-on is buried in the number', and the target then applies a 10% liquidity discount on top. Same-industry peer AGRS is discounted at 11.85%; BGTG at 12.95% with no explanation of the divergence. The grid shows COE -1pp takes the target to 45.7 before the discount, so together they are worth roughly 19 points.
challenges.answer: Removed the double count in the prose and re-based the premium: the 1.1pp is now described as the equity-risk-premium pin to the method card's IDR build (sovereign plus the house mid-band ERP), not a size or illiquidity add-on, and the only marketability charge is the house liquidity discount applied at the target. The 110bp gap to AGRS is explained as the pin applied at the issuer while the peer runs the engine default CAPM.

challenges.challenge: The HSC risk is cited to a document that does not contain it: S12 is the 383-name special-monitoring list and returns no hit for BGTG or Ganesha. The report also says the screen captures top holders above 92.5% while giving insider holdings of 89.4%, which would not qualify; and 89.4% insider plus 24.9% free float sums to 114%, which is impossible, so one of the two registry facts is wrong.
challenges.answer: The HSC claim is removed: the archived S12 announcement is paginated, so we neither claim nor deny BGTG's membership and treat index flow as a non-fundamental issue. Ownership is reconciled to single dated sources: the IDX-IC free float of 24.88% as of 4 November 2026 [S0] and the 2023 control disclosure [S13]; the report now says explicitly that the data pack's 89.4% insider figure overlaps the float and is not added to it.

challenges.challenge: Deck values are mis-rendered in the prose: the policy rate is printed as '575.0%' and consumer inflation as '328.0%' (deck: 5.75% and 3.28%), repeated in section 3; section 5 prints market capitalisation as 'IDR2,013,563,756,652.0bn' and turnover as 'IDR935,593,604.8bn' where the underlying values are Rp2.01tn and Rp0.94bn. Key drivers are therefore false as written in a reader-facing document.
challenges.answer: Re-rendered every affected figure from the deck in the right unit: the policy rate now prints 5.75% and consumer inflation 3.28% (they were multiplied by 100), market capitalisation prints IDR2,013.6bn and average daily turnover IDR0.9bn instead of the raw rupiah values scaled by bn. Checked sections 2, 3 and 5 for other percent and currency placeholders.

challenges.challenge: The 0% payout - which is why the DDM is zero-weighted and why the expected return is entirely book-driven - rests on S0 (a Yahoo extract) alone. The RUPST 2026 announcement (S3) is archived as a 434-character title-and-links stub with no resolutions, and that AGM is the document that would have declared or refused a FY2025 dividend. The 9M2025 PBT of Rp220.6bn cited as source-supported is a derived figure (290.609 less Q4 70.034) that S11 does not contain.
challenges.answer: The RUPST 2026 resolutions are archived as S14: whole FY2025 profit of Rp227.09bn retained, Rp1bn to the mandatory reserve, no dividend, Recovery Plan and board changes approved [S14]. The 0% payout now cites the AGM rather than the vendor extract. The 9M2025 PBT of Rp220.6bn is labelled derived (FY2025 less Q4 2025, both from the data pack) in section 3 rather than presented as a sourced line.

challenges.challenge: The packet prints 'bridge: net debt -1,026.8, minorities 0.0, associates 0.0' while bridge_items is empty and bridge is 0.0, so a reader naturally adds Rp42.8/share of cash to a value that already contains it inside book. Section 4 should say explicitly that bank cash is an operating asset and no bridge is applied.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says explicitly that a bank's cash is an operating asset, that the engine applies no bridge by design, and that the net cash the packet prints is the liquidity buffer rather than a distributable surplus added to book value.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says the scenarios are mirrored; the shocks are, but the values are not (bear -72% versus bull +88%), because the warranted multiple collapses non-linearly as ROE approaches g. Also the NOII line is called 'a fraction' of the prior year when the fall is 29%.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states the value asymmetry and its cause in one line: the shocks are mirrored but the values are not, because the warranted multiple is convex when ROE approaches terminal growth, so the same basis points are worth more on the downside. The NOII line is corrected from 'a fraction' to roughly three-tenths lower year on year.

missing_bull_case.note: Capital return and balance-sheet redeployment are named in section 4 ('the minority would own something close to book') and then valued at zero: net cash of Rp1,026.8bn is Rp42.8/share and Rp5.5tn of non-loan assets redeployed at a loan yield lifts NIM roughly 1.5pp. The bull is a pure mirror of the bear with no distribution, deployment, control or merger path.

missing_bear_case.note: No dilution path even though section 5 calls a discounted rights issue 'the standard mechanism' and 'live': share_change is 0.0 in every forecast year. No use of the 2027 KUR 0% relaxation or the Rp394tn programme-credit budget, which land directly on a 2.7%-growth MSME book, and no scenario where the special-mention stock (2.2% of loans) is charged.

assumption_realism.note: NOII is set at -5% (Rp86.9bn FY2026E) against a nine-month actual of Rp41.5bn, requiring Q4 of Rp45.4bn versus a 2026 quarterly run of Rp10.3-17.1bn. Long-run credit cost of 60bp sits below peer AGRS at 70bp and far below the Rp128.9bn special-mention stock. Terminal growth of 4% coexists with a 0% payout to FY2035E.

evidence_and_citations.note: S12 is the 383-name HSC list and contains no BGTG or Ganesha; 'Prima Tunas' appears in no archived source; the RUPST 2026 citation S3 is a 434-character link stub with no resolutions; the 9M2025 PBT of Rp220.6bn quoted in qc_justifications is derived (290.609 less 70.034) and labelled as sourced.

valuation_method_fit.note: Both weighted methods embed a 33% terminal payout (g 4% on a 6% ROE) while every explicit year to FY2035E has payout 0.0 and DPS 0, which is the report's own thesis. A 1.1pp COE premium and a 10% liquidity discount double-count illiquidity; the bridge prints net cash of -1,026.8 but applies nothing. Reverse DCF is unavailable in the engine yet asserted in prose.

bias_and_tone.note: The KBMI/class-upgrade driver is not in any source; 'fee income ... a fraction of the prior year' describes a 29% fall; and three unit slips (policy rate 575.0%, inflation 328.0%, market cap Rp2,013tn bn) make the prose assert more than the data. Direction is robust, magnitude is not.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck values are mis-rendered in sections 2 and 3 (5.75% and 3.28% printed as 575.0% and 328.0%). COE of 12.95% is 110bp above the same-industry peer AGRS at 11.85% with no explanation. The 2027 programme-credit and KUR relaxation news in the packet is not referenced at all.

conservatism_audit.note: Unsourced and all one way: 1.1pp COE premium, a 10% post-weighting liquidity discount, and 0% payout to 2035. Offsetting optimism the other way: inflated NOII, 60bp through-cycle CoR, rwa_density 1.00 versus peer 1.17. Net, they move the target by roughly 19 points and are not netted.

calibration.note: The ROE gate passes (FY2025A 6.37% vs model 6.12%, -0.24pp) and FY2026E PBT of Rp293.6bn reproduces the FY2025 actual of Rp290.6bn. But weights.changed remains justified-false with no qc_justifications entry, and the calibration.roe justification is an orphan resting on a comparative the source does not contain.

signoff.notes: SELL stands on substance. A 6.4% FY2025 ROE against a 12.95% COE, a 0% payout resolved by the RUPST, and a 0.5x-book price that implies about 9% sustainable ROE; warranted P/B 36 and residual income 20 both sit far below the Rp84 price and the Rp31 target has a wide margin. The 8 open FIXes do not change the rating: the FY2026E credit cost of 50bp rising to 70bp, and the 9.0% loan growth versus the ~11.5% implied by the 9M run-rate, are both, if corrected, adverse to value (lower ROE, lower book) and so reinforce rather than threaten the SELL; the remainder are text and citation fixes (AGM date 8 Oct vs S14's 26 May, the -76%/+94% asymmetry wording, a fifth vs 12.5%, the 61.8%/63.4% period mix, the S11 flat-PBT citation, the missing valuation.post_bs_review). Carry all eight into v2. Two structural notes for v2, neither rating-changing here: (i) the 60/40 P/B-primary split inverts the VAL_BANKS rule that residual income is the engine and warranted P/B the cross-check, and s4 does not argue the deviation; because P/B is the higher method this only raises the target, i.e. is conservative to a SELL; (ii) the rwa_density 1.00x basis says the securities book is both risk-weighted while the value treats RWA as the loan book alone - either the securities are SBN at ~0% RW and that should be stated, or the density should be nearer 2x, which would lower the bull's surplus-capital path but not the base SELL.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the last actual: NIM 3.85% vs 3.86% FY2025, ROE 6.1% vs 6.4%, payout 0% on the RUPST resolution [S14], NOII at the 9M2026 run-rate (Rp55.4bn vs Rp91.45bn FY2025) [S0]. Two small drifts offset: FY2026E loan growth 9.0% implies a flat Q4 against the 8.6% booked in 9M2026 (conservative ~2.5pp), while FY2026E credit cost 50bp is ~31bp below the FY2025 implied charge of ~81bp (optimistic). COE 12.95% = 10y SUN 7.45% + 5.5% ERP, mid-band of the house 5.0-6.0% [S0]. Scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers with base 50%; the values are not mirrored, explained in s5. Neither direction is stacked.

findings.finding: The report asserts the FY2025 profit retention was resolved at an AGM of 8 October 2026 (summary, s1, s4, s6, s7 and the assumptions payout basis). Its cited source S14 is dated 26 May 2026 and reports that meeting; 8 October is the S3 IR page posting timestamp. The meeting date as printed is contradicted by the source cited for the resolution.

loan_growth FY2026E 9.0% is stated to carry the 8.6% booked to September 2026 'into the fourth quarter at the same run-rate'. 5,820 to 6,320 is +8.6% over nine months; 6,343.8 at FY2026E implies Q4 growth of 0.4%, i.e. lending stalls for the quarter. The same run-rate gives about 11.5%, so the basis and the number disagree and the gap is unsourced conservatism on a key input.

credit_cost FY2026E is 50bp but the same basis computes the FY2025 implied charge at ~80bp (revenue Rp510.16bn less opex at 33.8% and PBT Rp290.61bn leaves Rp47.2bn = 81bp of 5,820). The text then says the 70bp through-cycle rate 'sits above the current flow, not at it', which is false against their own 81bp. FY2026E is therefore 31bp below the last actual with no source.

s5 states 'the bear loses more than the bull gains'. Model output: bear 7.97 (-76% vs base 33.20), bull 64.26 (+94%). The bull gains more in both percentage and rupiah terms, so the stated direction of the asymmetry, and the convexity explanation attached to it, are wrong.

The investment summary says 'the residual-income run says roughly a fifth of book'. The engine's residual-income value is Rp19.92 on BVPS Rp159.78, i.e. 12.5% of book (an eighth). The multiple method is 22.3% ('about a quarter'), which is correct.

The summary pairs FY2025 equity Rp3,689.3bn and FY2025 loans Rp5,820.0bn (63.4%) with a 'capital ratio near 61.8%', which is the FY2026E car_est (Rp3,923.1bn / Rp6,343.8bn). Separately, rwa_density 1.00x says RWA approx loans, but its basis describes 'loans plus a securities portfolio of similar size, both risk-weighted', which would be ~2.0x. The basis contradicts the parameter.

The extreme_call justification supports 'nine-month-2026 PBT flat year on year' with [S11], but S11 carries the 9M2026 PBT (Rp224.61bn) and no prior-year comparative. The flat claim is derived from [S0]: FY2025 PBT Rp290.61bn less 2025Q4 Rp70.03bn = Rp220.58bn, so 9M2026 is +1.8%.

valuation.post_bs_review is absent from fund record although the method card requires a note and sources for what was searched after the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date. The substance (30 October results release S11, HSC announcement S12, AGM payout S14) is discussed in the report but is not recorded in the field the engine and reviewers read.

weights.changed WARN is unaddressed in the engine (justified: false) and the 60/40 split inverts the VAL_BANKS card, which designates residual income as the engine and warranted P/BV as the cross-check. weights_basis argues the change and the inversion is the less bearish choice, so it is not a stacking concern, but the gate reads as unresolved.
s1 calls 9M2026 fee income 'roughly a quarter lower year on year'; s3 says 'roughly three-tenths'. The derived figures are 41.55 vs 58.48 = -29%, so three-tenths is the accurate description.

flags.message: expected return -63%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the negative return: (1) sustainable ROE of about 6% - FY2025 ROE 6.4% [S10][S0] with nine-month-2026 PBT flat year on year [S11], against a 12.95% COE built from the 7.45% 10-year SUN plus a 5.5% ERP; (2) a 0% payout with no dividend ever paid [S0], so the minority gets no cash return while book compounds below COE; (3) the price capitalises 0.55x book for a bank whose warranted multiple at that spread is a fifth of book. Today's Rp84 price implies a sustainable ROE of about 8.9% at the same COE and 4% growth - a level BGTG has never earned, so the reverse-DCF gap is the thesis rather than an artefact of the terminal value.
